title: Reorder List
description: Three classic linked-list moves stitched together: find the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, then weave the two halves node-by-node.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: given a singly linked list L0 → L1 → … → Ln-1 → Ln, reorder it to L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → L2 → Ln-2 → … In words: interleave the front-to-back walk with the back-to-front walk. So [1,2,3,4,5] becomes [1,5,2,4,3]."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Modify in place — rewrite next pointers — or return a new list?
• Even-length list ([1,2,3,4]) — result is [1,4,2,3] (the middle two end up adjacent)?
• Empty list — return null without doing anything?
• Single node — return as-is?
• Two-node list ([1,2]) — already in the target form (first + last), no work needed?
sections.why: The even-vs-odd-length question is the one most candidates skip and regret. For odd length [1,2,3,4,5], the middle node (3) ends up alone at the tail. For even length [1,2,3,4], the middle pair (2,3) ends up as the last two nodes. Both cases need to fall out naturally from the same code, and the 'where exactly is the midpoint?' decision is what makes that happen. The 'modify in place' question matters for space — in-place is O(1) extra; copying to an array first is O(n) extra.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the array-buffer solution before you discard it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is: walk the list and push every node into an array, then use two indices (l from 0, r from n-1) walking inward, building a fresh linked list by alternating arr[l], arr[r], arr[l+1], arr[r-1], etc. O(n) time, O(n) extra space for the array.

The optimization is to avoid the array by exploiting linked-list operations directly: find the midpoint, reverse the second half in place, then weave the two halves together by rewriting next pointers. Same O(n) time, but O(1) extra space because we're just shuffling existing pointers — no new allocations."
sections.why: Two reasons to name the array brute force. (1) It proves you can solve the problem without composing three linked-list primitives — important because the in-place version requires significant linked-list muscle and if you go straight there without acknowledging the simpler alternative, the interviewer may worry you don't have a fallback. (2) Framing the in-place version as 'same work, just done with pointers instead of an array' justifies the cleverness rather than presenting it as magic. The array approach is what makes the structure obvious; the pointer approach is what makes it space-efficient.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to find-middle + reverse-second-half + weave?
sections.say:
"This is three classic linked-list primitives stitched together, and recognizing that decomposition is the whole game. The target [1,5,2,4,3] (from [1,2,3,4,5]) is exactly 'walk the first half forward, interleaved with walking the second half backward'. So:

Primitive 1 — find the middle with slow/fast pointers. With the guard `fast.next && fast.next.next`, slow ends at the LAST node of the first half. (For [1,2,3,4,5]: slow ends at 3. For [1,2,3,4]: slow ends at 2.) That's convenient because I can then cut with `slow.next = null` and treat slow's first half cleanly.

Primitive 2 — reverse the second half in place. Start at slow.next, apply the standard three-pointer reverse dance, get back the new head of the reversed second half.

Primitive 3 — weave. Now I have two lists: `a` (first half, head = original head) and `b` (reversed second half). The weave loop walks both, splicing b's next-node into a's chain: `a.next = b; b.next = a.next.cached; advance both`. Loop while `b` is non-null because the reversed second half is the shorter-or-equal of the two — when nodes are odd-count, the first half has one extra and that extra is already correctly positioned at the tail.

The whole thing is O(n) — three linear passes — and O(1) space."
sections.why: Naming the three primitives is the move. 'It's three things glued together' is what unlocks the problem — once you see the decomposition, each piece is a sub-problem you've already solved (find middle = LeetCode 876, reverse list = LeetCode 206, weave is the only new bit). Saying it out loud also signals to the interviewer that you've connected this problem to its building blocks, which is exactly the kind of pattern-composition skill they're hiring for. Calling out 'loop on b because it's the shorter half' upfront prevents the most common bug — looping on a, which over-extends past the original midpoint and creates infinite loops or wrong wiring.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the three-phase model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure the midpoint and weave behave right for odd vs even length." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — odd length (asymmetric weave), even length (symmetric weave), and the trivial early-exit single-node case.

examples.note: Odd length — middle node (3) ends up at the tail. Weave runs 2 times (length of reversed second half).
examples.trace:
phase 1: slow/fast. slow ends at 3 (last of first half).
phase 2: reverse from 4. cut: 3.next=null. reverse: [4,5] → [5,4]. 
  Now firstHalf = [1,2,3], reversedSecondHalf = [5,4]
phase 3: weave. a=1, b=5.
  iter1: an=2, bn=4. 1.next=5, 5.next=2. a=2, b=4. → [1,5,2,3] (so far)
  iter2: an=3, bn=null. 2.next=4, 4.next=3. a=3, b=null. → [1,5,2,4,3]
  loop exit (b=null). return head → [1,5,2,4,3]

examples.note: Even length — slow lands at 2 (last of first half). Weave runs 2 times symmetrically.
examples.trace:
phase 1: slow/fast. slow ends at 2 (last of first half).
phase 2: reverse from 3. cut: 2.next=null. reverse: [3,4] → [4,3].
  Now firstHalf = [1,2], reversedSecondHalf = [4,3]
phase 3: weave. a=1, b=4.
  iter1: an=2, bn=3. 1.next=4, 4.next=2. a=2, b=3. → [1,4,2] (so far)
  iter2: an=null, bn=null. 2.next=3, 3.next=null. a=null, b=null. → [1,4,2,3]
  loop exit (b=null). return head → [1,4,2,3]

examples.note: Early-exit case — head.next is null, so the function returns immediately without entering the three phases.

sections.why: Tracing surfaces three specific bugs. (1) The odd-length case ([1,2,3,4,5]) confirms the middle node ends up at the tail naturally — no special handling needed because the weave loop drives on `b` (the shorter half) and stops one iteration before the first half is fully consumed. (2) The even-length case ([1,2,3,4]) confirms the weave terminates cleanly when both halves are the same length — both `a` and `b` reach null simultaneously. (3) The single-node early exit confirms the guard at the top (`if (!head || !head.next) return head`) prevents a null-deref in phase 1 (where `fast.next.next` would throw on a 1-node list).

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Empty list (head = null) → guard catches it, return null. ✓
• Single node → guard catches it, return as-is. ✓
• Two nodes ([1,2]) → guard at top doesn't catch (head.next is not null), but the phase 1 loop condition `fast.next && fast.next.next` is false from the start, so slow stays at 1. Phase 2: reverse from 2, cut 1.next=null. firstHalf=[1], reversed=[2]. Phase 3: weave, a=1, b=2. iter1: 1.next=2, 2.next=null. b=null. → [1,2]. Already in target form. ✓
• Three nodes ([1,2,3]) → expected output [1,3,2]. slow ends at 2 after one fast-step. reverse from 3 → [3]. weave: 1.next=3, 3.next=2 (since an=null? wait — an=2.next.next-original = null but a was already cached). Let me re-walk: a=1, b=3. an=null, bn=null. 1.next=3, 3.next=null. a=null, b=null. Now full list: 1→3→2 because 2 was cut off but the cached an picked it up. Actually no — let me re-check: after phase 2, the first half is just [1,2] and 2.next=null (we cut at slow=2 which was the last of first half… wait, for n=3, fast.next.next-from-1 = 3, fast.next-from-1=2, so guard is true once, slow=2, fast=3. Then guard: fast.next=null → false. slow ends at 2. We then `slow.next = null` so firstHalf=[1,2]. reverse [3] → [3]. weave a=1, b=3. an=2, bn=null. 1.next=3, 3.next=2. a=2, b=null. Result: 1→3→2 ✓. So the trace works — the cached `an` is what carries node 2 forward.
• Even count where both halves are exactly equal in length — handled (see trace [1,2,3,4]).
• Very long list → O(n) time across all three phases, O(1) space. The three phases are sequential, so total work is 3n which is still linear."
sections.why: Walking the 2-node and 3-node cases out loud is what shows you've stress-tested the smallest non-trivial inputs. Most candidates write the algorithm assuming 'large enough' lists and then crash on n=2 because they don't realize the phase 1 loop doesn't even run. The 3-node trace is also where the cached `an = a.next` insight earns its keep — without caching, the weave's `a.next = b` would lose access to node 2 immediately, and the result would be [1,3] instead of [1,3,2].

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) total. Phase 1 (find middle) walks half the list — n/2 nodes. Phase 2 (reverse second half) also walks n/2. Phase 3 (weave) walks the reversed second half — n/2 again. Sum: 3 × n/2 = 1.5n, which is O(n). Three sequential linear passes, no nested loops.

Space is O(1) — no auxiliary data structures, just a handful of pointer variables (slow, fast, prev, curr, nxt, a, b, an, bn). All rewiring is in place on the existing nodes.

If you wanted to extend, the three primitives apply elsewhere: 'find middle' is LeetCode 876 standalone, 'reverse list' is LeetCode 206 standalone, and 'palindrome linked list' (LeetCode 234) uses find-middle + reverse-second-half + compare. Reorder List is the composition; once you've drilled the three pieces individually, this falls out as glue."
sections.why: The 1.5n arithmetic is the clean defense of O(n) — it makes explicit that 'three linear passes' is still linear, which matters because some interviewers will push back with 'isn't doing three things sequentially worse than one thing?'. The answer is no, because they're additive, not multiplicative. The Palindrome Linked List extension is the natural follow-up and proves you see find-middle + reverse-half as a reusable composition rather than this problem's specific trick — that's how the three-phase pattern shows up across the linked-list family.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the three-move dance: find midpoint, reverse second half, then weave. Input is an array. Watch the list split into firstHalf + reversedSecondHalf, then interleave node by node.
trace: const toList = (arr) => { const d = { val: 0, next: null }; let c = d; for (const v of arr) { c.next = { val: v, next: null }; c = c.next; } return d.next; };
const toArr = (h) => { const o = []; let cnt = 0; while (h && cnt < 50) { o.push(h.val); h = h.next; cnt++; } return o; };
yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — list=${JSON.stringify(input)}`, state: { input } };
yield { line: 2, label: 'early exit — list has 0 or 1 nodes', state: { list: toArr(head), returns: JSON.stringify(toArr(head)) } };
yield { line: 4, label: 'init slow=head, fast=head', state: { list: toArr(head), slowVal: slow.val, fastVal: fast.val } };
yield { line: 7, label: `advance — slow=${slow.val}, fast=${fast.val}`, state: { list: toArr(head), slowVal: slow.val, fastVal: fast.val } };
yield { line: 8, label: `midpoint found — slow=${slow.val} (last node of first half)`, state: { list: toArr(head), slowVal: slow.val } };
yield { line: 10, label: `set prev=null, curr=slow.next (${curr ? curr.val : 'null'}) — start of second half`, state: { firstHalf: toArr(head), curr: curr ? curr.val : null } };
yield { line: 11, label: 'cut the list — slow.next=null', state: { firstHalf: toArr(head), secondHalf: toArr(curr) } };
yield { line: 16, label: `reverse step — prev=${prev.val}, curr=${curr ? curr.val : 'null'}`, state: { firstHalf: toArr(head), reversedSoFar: toArr(prev), curr: curr ? curr.val : null } };
yield { line: 17, label: `reverse done — reversedSecondHalf=${JSON.stringify(toArr(prev))}`, state: { firstHalf: toArr(head), reversedSecondHalf: toArr(prev) } };
yield { line: 19, label: `weave init — a=${a.val}, b=${b ? b.val : 'null'}`, state: { firstHalf: toArr(head), reversedSecondHalf: toArr(prev), aVal: a.val, bVal: b ? b.val : null } };
yield { line: 25, label: `weave iter ${iter} — woven so far`, state: { woven: toArr(head), aVal: a ? a.val : null, bVal: b ? b.val : null } };
if (iter > 30) { yield { line: 25, label: 'safety stop', state: { returns: JSON.stringify(toArr(head)) } }; return; }
yield { line: 27, label: 'return head', state: { result: toArr(head), returns: JSON.stringify(toArr(head)) } };

notes: Slow/fast with the guard `fast.next && fast.next.next` leaves slow at the LAST node of the first half — convenient for cutting.
Cut with `slow.next = null` BEFORE reversing, so the first half terminates cleanly.
Weave loop condition uses `b` (the shorter/equal half) — when nodes are odd, the first half has one extra node already in place.
Cache `a.next` and `b.next` before rewiring or you lose the rest of each list.

questions.q: After slow/fast with guard `fast.next && fast.next.next`, where does slow land?
options: At the last node of the first half (works for cutting)
At the first node of the second half

questions.q: Why set slow.next = null before reversing?
options: So the first half has a clean termination and the reversal walks only the second half

questions.q: Which half drives the weave loop?
options: The reversed second half (b) — it is the shorter-or-equal of the two

exercises.prompt: Fill in the three moves: midpoint, reverse, weave. First blank is the full double-hop expression.

blanks.hint: fast advances by two — the full double-hop expression
cut the list cleanly between the halves before reversing
flip the pointer backward — the central rewrite of reverse
drive on the reversed second half; it is the shorter-or-equal of the two

L3.prompt: Write `reorderList(head)` that reorders `L0→L1→…→Ln` to `L0→Ln→L1→Ln-1→…`. Use toList/toArr helpers and log `JSON.stringify(toArr(reorderList(toList([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))))`.
hints: Three steps: midpoint (slow/fast), reverse the second half, weave.
Cut with slow.next = null before reversing.
Weave while b is non-null; cache a.next and b.next each iteration.
